title: 01-basics
text:
R is a programming language designed primarily for statistical computing, data analysis, and visualization.
This chapter introduces the basic syntax and operations used in R.

title: 01-basics
text:
Assignment Operator
We can also use = operator for assignment:

x = 20
x

[1] 20


However, <- is the most conventional assignment operator in R.

title: Data Types
text:
Every value in R has a type. Understanding data types is important because different types behave differently when we perform calculations, comparisons, or transformations.
The most common basic data types in R are:

Numeric
Integer
Character
Logical
Complex

R also has special values such as NA, NULL, NaN, and Inf.

title: Data Types
text:
Example

price <- 19.99
temperature <- 23.5
average <- 87.25

title: Data Types
text:
Combining strings
Use paste():

first_name <- "Sujan"
last_name <- "Karna"

paste(first_name, last_name)

[1] "Sujan Karna"


Or use paste0():

paste0(first_name, "_", last_name)

[1] "Sujan_Karna"


The difference is that paste() inserts a separator by default, while paste0() does not.

paste("Hello", "World")

[1] "Hello World"

paste0("Hello", "World")

[1] "HelloWorld"

title: Data Types
text:
Logical expressions
Comparisons produce logical values:

x <- 20

x > 10

[1] TRUE

x < 10

[1] FALSE

x == 20

[1] TRUE

x != 20

[1] FALSE


Output:
TRUE
FALSE
TRUE
FALSE

title: Data Types
text:
typeof()
typeof() tells you the underlying storage type.

x <- 10
typeof(x)

[1] "double"

title: Data Types
Data Types
text:
Type-checking functions
R provides functions that return TRUE or FALSE.

is.numeric(10)

[1] TRUE

is.character("Hello")

[1] TRUE

is.logical(TRUE)

[1] TRUE

is.integer(10L)

[1] TRUE


Some other useful functions:

is.double(10)

[1] TRUE

is.complex(2 + 3i)

[1] TRUE

title: Data Types
text:
Convert to numeric

x <- "100"

as.numeric(x)

[1] 100


Check:

typeof(as.numeric(x))

[1] "double"

title: Data Types
text:
Convert to character

x <- 100

as.character(x)

[1] "100"

title: Data Types
text:
Convert to integer

x <- 10.5

as.integer(x)

[1] 10


Note that conversion to integer removes the decimal part rather than rounding the value.

as.integer(10.9)

[1] 10

as.integer(10.1)

[1] 10

title: Data Types
text:
Convert to logical

as.logical(1)

[1] TRUE

as.logical(0)

[1] FALSE

title: Data Types
text:
NA
NA represents a missing value.

x <- c(10, 20, NA, 40)

x

[1] 10 20 NA 40


Check for missing values:

is.na(x)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE


This returns:
FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE

title: Data Types
text:
NULL
NULL represents the absence of a value.

x <- NULL

x

NULL


Check:

is.null(x)

[1] TRUE


NULL is different from NA.

NA means a value is missing.
NULL means there is no value.

title: Data Types
text:
NaN
NaN means Not a Number.
It can occur when an undefined numerical operation is performed.

0 / 0

[1] NaN


Check:

is.nan(0 / 0)

[1] TRUE

title: Data Types
text:
Inf
Inf represents positive infinity.

1 / 0

[1] Inf


Negative infinity:

-1 / 0

[1] -Inf


Check:

is.infinite(1 / 0)

[1] TRUE

title: 03-vectors
text:
A vector is one of the fundamental data structures in R.
A vector stores multiple values of the same basic data type.
For example:

numbers <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

numbers

[1] 10 20 30 40 50


The function c() means combine or concatenate.

c(10, 20, 30, 40)

[1] 10 20 30 40


creates a vector containing four values.

Important: R uses 1-based indexing, meaning the first element is at position 1.

title: 03-vectors
text:
Using c()
The most common way to create a vector is with c().

numbers <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

numbers

[1] 10 20 30 40 50


Character vector:

names <- c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie")

names

[1] "Alice"   "Bob"     "Charlie"


Logical vector:

passed <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)

passed

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE

title: 03-vectors
text:
Selecting Multiple Elements
Use a vector of positions.

numbers[c(1, 3, 5)]

[1] 10 30 50


Result:
10 30 50
Select a range:

numbers[2:4]

[1] 20 30 40


Result:
20 30 40

title: 03-vectors
text:
order()
order() returns the positions that would sort the vector.

x <- c(40, 10, 50, 20, 30)

order(x)

[1] 2 4 5 1 3


You can use it to reorder the vector:

x[order(x)]

[1] 10 20 30 40 50


Descending:

x[order(x, decreasing = TRUE)]

[1] 50 40 30 20 10



Difference: sort() returns sorted values, while order() returns their positions.

title: 03-vectors
text:
any()
Checks whether at least one element satisfies a condition.

x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)

any(x > 45)

[1] TRUE

title: 03-vectors
text:
all()
Checks whether all elements satisfy a condition.

all(x > 5)

[1] TRUE


Another example:

all(x > 20)

[1] FALSE

title: 03-vectors
text:
Inspect

length(x)

[1] 3

typeof(x)

[1] "character"

class(x)

[1] "character"

is.vector(x)

[1] TRUE

title: 03-vectors
text:
Analyze

x = as.numeric(x)
x

[1] 100   3 200

sum(x)

[1] 303

mean(x)

[1] 101

median(x)

[1] 100

min(x)

[1] 3

max(x)

[1] 200

sd(x)

[1] 98.50381

title: 03-vectors
text:
Transform

sort(x)

[1]   3 100 200

sort(x, decreasing = TRUE)

[1] 200 100   3

rev(x)

[1] 200   3 100

unique(x)

[1] 100   3 200

title: 03-vectors
text:
Search

which(x > 20)

[1] 1 3

any(x > 20)

[1] TRUE

all(x > 20)

[1] FALSE

title: 03-vectors
text:
Missing Values

is.na(x)

[1] FALSE FALSE FALSE

sum(is.na(x))

[1] 0

mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 101

title: 04-matrices
text:
A matrix is a two-dimensional data structure in R.
A matrix consists of:

Rows
Columns
Elements

Unlike a data frame, all elements in a matrix normally have the same basic data type.
For example:

matrix(
  c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  nrow = 2,
  ncol = 3
)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6


This creates:
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6

title: 04-matrices
text:
Fill by Row
Use byrow = TRUE.

matrix(
  1:6,
  nrow = 2,
  ncol = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6


Result:
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6

Remember: By default, R fills matrices by column.

title: 04-matrices
text:
Number of Rows

nrow(m)

[1] 2

title: 04-matrices
text:
Number of Columns

ncol(m)

[1] 3

title: 04-matrices
text:
Number of Elements

length(m)

[1] 6

title: 04-matrices
text:
Multiplication by a Scalar

A * 2

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    2    4
[2,]    6    8


Every element is multiplied by 2.

title: 04-matrices
text:
Row Sums

rowSums(scores)

[1] 240 255 270

title: 04-matrices
text:
Column Sums

colSums(scores)

[1] 255 253 257

title: 04-matrices
text:
Row Means

rowMeans(scores)

[1] 80 85 90

title: 04-matrices
text:
Column Means

colMeans(scores)

[1] 85.00000 84.33333 85.66667

title: 04-matrices
text:
Apply a Function to Rows

apply(scores, 1, mean)

[1] 80 85 90

title: 04-matrices
text:
Apply a Function to Columns

apply(scores, 2, mean)

[1] 85.00000 84.33333 85.66667


For example:

apply(scores, 1, max)

[1] 90 95 92


finds the maximum value in each row.

title: 04-matrices
text:
rbind()
rbind() means row bind.

A <- matrix(
  1:4,
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

B <- matrix(
  5:8,
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

rbind(A, B)

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    2
[2,]    3    4
[3,]    5    6
[4,]    7    8


This adds rows.

title: 04-matrices
text:
cbind()
cbind() means column bind.

cbind(A, B)

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    1    2    5    6
[2,]    3    4    7    8


This adds columns.

title: 04-matrices
text:
Exercise 4 — Matrix Multiplication
Create:

A <- matrix(
  c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  nrow = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

B <- matrix(
  c(5, 6, 7, 8),

Pay attention to the difference between * and %*%.

title: 05-lists
text:
A list is a flexible R data structure that can contain multiple objects, including objects of different types.
Unlike a vector, which normally contains values of the same basic type, a list can contain:

Numbers
Character strings
Logical values
Vectors
Matrices
Other lists
Data frames
Functions
Other R objects

For example:

person <- list(
  name = "Sujan",
  age = 25,
  student = TRUE
)

person

$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE


This list contains a character value, a numeric value, and a logical value.

Key idea: A vector is usually homogeneous, while a list can contain heterogeneous objects.

title: 05-lists
text:
Example

person[1]

$name
[1] "Sujan"


returns a list.

person[[1]]

[1] "Sujan"


returns:
"Sujan"

title: 05-lists
text:
First element

student[1]

$name
[1] "Sujan"


Returns a list.

title: 05-lists
text:
First element’s value

student[[1]]

[1] "Sujan"


Returns the actual value.

title: 05-lists
text:
Name

student$name

[1] "Sujan"

title: 05-lists
text:
Name using [[ ]]

student[["name"]]

[1] "Sujan"

title: 05-lists
text:
First score

student$scores[1]

[1] 80

title: 05-lists
text:
All scores

student$scores

[1] 80 90 85

title: 05-lists
text:
Second score

student[["scores"]][2]

[1] 90

title: 05-lists
text:
names()
Get or set names.

student <- list(
  "Sujan",
  25,
  TRUE
)

names(student) <- c(
  "name",
  "age",
  "student"
)

student

$name
[1] "Sujan"

$age
[1] 25

$student
[1] TRUE

title: 05-lists
text:
length()
Get the number of top-level elements.

length(student)

[1] 3

title: 05-lists
text:
str()
Inspect the structure.

str(student)

List of 3
 $ name   : chr "Sujan"
 $ age    : num 25
 $ student: logi TRUE

title: 05-lists
text:
unlist()
Convert a list into a simpler vector when possible.

unlist(student)

   name     age student 
"Sujan"    "25"  "TRUE"

title: 05-lists
text:
is.list()
Check whether an object is a list.

is.list(student)

[1] TRUE
